Kinship, descent and alliance together form an important part of the social organization of many societies.

Kinship performs several functions: it determines who can marry whom, decides descent and inheritance, assigns rights and duties, provides social security, regulates behaviour through kinship usages, and in tribal societies may also organize political and economic life.

Kinship usages: avoidance (for example, restrictions on contact between a man and his wife's mother in some societies), joking relationship (permitted teasing, for example between a person and the sibling of their spouse), teknonymy (referring to a person through their child's name), avunculate and amitate, and couvade (a custom in which the husband imitates or observes restrictions during his wife's childbirth).

Mizo society is organized into clans and sub-clans traced through the male line, and clan identity has historically been important for social identity and relationships. Patrilineal descent determines the clan name a child inherits.

Kinship remains important even in modern society, particularly at times of marriage, death, festivals and crisis. In India, kin networks also play a role in migration, employment and political support.

sections.title: Religion: Nature, Functions, Types and Secularism

blocks.text:
Religion is an important social institution involving beliefs and practices related to sacred or spiritual realities. It usually includes rituals, moral ideas, symbols and collective practices shared by a community.

Religion performs several social functions. It can provide meaning and emotional support, strengthen group solidarity, transmit moral values and create a sense of collective identity. Religious rituals may bring members together and reinforce common beliefs.

Religions vary in beliefs, practices and forms of organization. Sociology is mainly concerned with religion as a social phenomenon: how religious beliefs and institutions influence social life and how social conditions influence religious practices.

Secularism concerns the relationship between religion and public life. In a socially and religiously diverse society, secular arrangements seek to provide a common civic framework without making one religious tradition the exclusive basis of public authority. Religion and secularism therefore remain important themes in understanding modern social institutions.

Durkheim's study of totemism among Australian aborigines led him to argue that religion is essentially social: rituals create 'collective effervescence', a feeling of shared excitement and unity that renews social solidarity.

Weber's sociology of religion studied world religions such as Hinduism, Buddhism, Confucianism and Judaism, as well as Protestantism, to show how religious ideas influence economic behaviour. Marx saw religion as a reflection of material conditions and a tool of ideological control.
Religion can be both integrative and divisive. It unites believers, but it can also divide society along religious lines and lead to communal conflict when used for political purposes.

In Mizoram, Christianity, introduced by missionaries beginning with J.H. Lorrain and F.W. Savidge in 1894 and followed by Welsh Presbyterian missionaries, has deeply shaped social life. The church influences education, festivals, music, social norms and community organization. Christmas and New Year are the major festivals, and churches play a key role in social welfare.

Social processes are recurring forms of interaction through which individuals and groups relate to one another. They may promote unity and adjustment or create opposition and tension. Social processes are continuous and change according to social conditions.

Ogburn and Nimkoff defined social process as 'the ways in which individuals and groups interact and establish relationships'. Social processes are the dynamic aspect of society, while social structure is the static aspect.

The two main categories are associative or conjunctive processes (cooperation, accommodation, assimilation) and dissociative or disjunctive processes (competition, conflict). Some writers also include acculturation, integration and isolation.
Social processes are universal, found in all societies, but their form and intensity differ from one culture to another.

sections.title: Continuity and Change in Social Processes

blocks.text: Social interaction contains both continuity and change. Established relationships and institutions provide continuity, while new interests, conflicts, technology and changing conditions modify patterns of interaction.
Continuity in social processes is maintained by customs, traditions, institutions and socialization, which ensure that the same forms of interaction are repeated across generations.

Change in social processes arises from new technology, economic development, migration, education, political movements and contact with other cultures. For example, competition in education and employment has increased with the expansion of formal education and limited job opportunities.
Sociologists see continuity and change not as opposites but as two aspects of the same social reality. Even when new forms emerge, they often combine with older patterns.

Accommodation is a process by which individuals or groups adjust to conflict or differences in order to maintain workable relations. It may reduce open hostility without completely removing the underlying differences.

MacIver and Page describe accommodation as the process in which a person 'attains a sense of harmony with his environment'. Ogburn and Nimkoff called it the term used for 'the adjustment of hostile individuals or groups'.

Methods of accommodation include coercion (the stronger party forces the weaker to accept terms), compromise (both parties give up some demands), arbitration and mediation (a third party helps settle the dispute), conciliation (attempts to reconcile parties), toleration (living with differences), conversion (one party adopts the views of the other) and sublimation (redirecting hostile feelings into constructive channels).

Examples include peace accords between governments and insurgent groups, agreements between trade unions and management, and the caste system as a form of accommodation between unequal groups. The Mizo Peace Accord of 1986 between the Government of India and the Mizo National Front is often cited as an example of accommodation that ended a long conflict.
Assimilation is a social process in which individuals or groups gradually share common cultural patterns and become more closely integrated. It generally develops through prolonged social contact.

Robert E. Park and Ernest W. Burgess defined assimilation as 'a process of interpenetration and fusion in which persons and groups acquire the memories, sentiments and attitudes of other persons or groups and, by sharing their experience and history, are incorporated with them in a common cultural life'.

Factors that help assimilation include tolerance, intimate social contact, intermarriage, cultural similarity, equal economic opportunity and shared education. Factors that hinder it include isolation, physical or cultural differences, prejudice, discrimination and a feeling of superiority or inferiority.

Assimilation is a slow, unconscious and two-way process. Critics argue that forced assimilation can destroy minority cultures, so many modern societies prefer pluralism or multiculturalism, which allows groups to keep their identities while living together.

Cooperation is a process in which individuals or groups work together for common interests or objectives. It is essential for family life, institutions, economic activity and wider social organization.

Green defined cooperation as 'the continuous and common endeavour of two or more persons to perform a task or to reach a goal that is commonly cherished'. Cooperation may be direct (people working together, such as farmers harvesting jointly) or indirect (people doing different tasks for a common end, as in the division of labour).

MacIver and Page also distinguished primary cooperation (in primary groups), secondary cooperation (in secondary groups such as offices) and tertiary cooperation (temporary cooperation between groups for convenience).

In traditional Mizo villages, community work for the village such as clearing paths, building houses and helping in jhum cultivation reflected strong cooperation, supported by the value of tlawmngaihna. The YMA continues similar community service today.

Conflict is a social process in which individuals or groups oppose one another because of incompatible interests, values, goals or claims. Conflict can be personal or collective and may produce both disruption and social change.
Gillin and Gillin defined conflict as 'the social process in which individuals or groups seek their ends by directly challenging the antagonist by violence or threat of violence'.

Types of conflict include personal conflict, racial conflict, class conflict, political conflict, international conflict, and communal or ethnic conflict. Conflict can be latent (hidden) or manifest (open).

Karl Marx saw class conflict as the driving force of history. Lewis Coser, in 'The Functions of Social Conflict' (1956), argued that conflict can also have positive functions, such as strengthening group unity, clarifying issues and bringing about necessary reforms. Ralf Dahrendorf linked conflict to the unequal distribution of authority in organizations.

Competition occurs when individuals or groups seek the same limited goal, position or resource. Unlike direct conflict, competitors may not always confront one another personally. Competition is common in education, employment, economy and politics.

Biesanz and Biesanz defined competition as 'the striving of two or more persons for the same goal which is limited so that all cannot share it'. Competition is generally impersonal, continuous, universal and governed by rules.
Types of competition include economic (for jobs and markets), cultural, competition for social position and status, racial, and political competition (between parties in elections).

Competition has positive effects such as motivation, efficiency and innovation, but excessive competition can lead to stress, frustration, inequality and conflict. When competition becomes personal and the rules are broken, it may turn into conflict.

Hegemony refers to dominance maintained not only through direct force but also through influence, accepted ideas and social leadership. A dominant group may secure consent by making its values or worldview appear normal or legitimate.

The concept of hegemony was developed by the Italian Marxist thinker Antonio Gramsci (1891-1937) in his 'Prison Notebooks'. He argued that the ruling class maintains power not only through the state's coercive apparatus (police, army) but also through civil society (schools, church, media, family), which spreads ideas that make the existing order appear natural and common sense.

Gramsci argued that challenging hegemony requires 'counter-hegemony', in which subordinate groups develop their own ideas and organisations. He gave an important role to 'organic intellectuals' who emerge from and express the interests of the working class.

The concept is used to study gender (patriarchal hegemony), culture (the dominance of Western media), language and caste. Hegemony is treated as a dissociative process because it involves unequal power, even though it may appear peaceful.
Social disorganization refers to the weakening or breakdown of established social relationships, norms or institutions, producing difficulty in maintaining social order and effective regulation.

Elliott and Merrill defined social disorganization as 'the process by which the relationships between members of a group are broken or dissolved'. W.I. Thomas and Florian Znaniecki, in 'The Polish Peasant in Europe and America', described it as a decrease in the influence of existing social rules of behaviour upon individual members of the group.
The concept was developed by the Chicago School of Sociology, which studied crime, delinquency and family breakdown in rapidly growing American cities in the early twentieth century.
Social disorganization is the opposite of social organization. It is always relative, because every society has some degree of disorganization.
Social disorganization may arise from rapid social change, conflict between norms, economic problems, migration, breakdown of institutions and other conditions that weaken social regulation.

Durkheim linked disorganization with anomie, a state of normlessness during rapid social change. Ogburn explained it through cultural lag, when material culture changes faster than non-material culture.

Other causes include natural disasters, wars, economic depression, unemployment, rapid urbanization, migration, conflict of values between generations, breakdown of family and community controls, and the spread of drugs and alcohol.

In north-eastern India, problems such as substance abuse, HIV/AIDS and unemployment among youth have been studied as examples of social problems that may reflect weakening social controls and rapid change.
It may involve weakened social control, conflicting norms, instability, poor coordination between institutions and difficulty in maintaining accepted patterns of behaviour.

Elliott and Merrill identified three levels of disorganization: personal disorganization (such as crime, alcoholism, suicide and mental illness), family disorganization (such as desertion, divorce and conflict) and community disorganization (such as poverty, unemployment, crime and corruption).

Signs of disorganization include a conflict of mores and institutions, the transfer of functions from one group to another, individualization (people pursuing their own interests without regard to the group), changes in the role and status of individuals, and a lack of consensus on values.
These characteristics appear in different combinations in different societies and must be studied in their specific context.

Measures may include strengthening social institutions, improving education and welfare, reducing severe social and economic inequalities, effective community organization and appropriate formal social control.

Remedies include social planning that anticipates the effects of change, family welfare and counselling services, de-addiction and rehabilitation programmes, youth employment schemes, strengthening community organizations, legal reforms, and value education in schools.

Community-based organizations, churches and NGOs play an important role. In Mizoram, the YMA and churches have been active in anti-drug campaigns and community welfare, showing how civil society can help reduce disorganization.

A balanced approach combines informal social control (family, community, religion) with formal measures (law, police, welfare schemes), while addressing the root causes such as poverty and inequality.

sections.title: Social Processes: Meaning, Characteristics, Continuity and Change

blocks.text:
Social processes are recurring patterns of interaction through which individuals and groups establish, maintain or change social relationships. Human society is based on interaction, and repeated forms of interaction develop into recognizable social processes.

Social processes have several characteristics. They arise through interaction, occur continuously, involve individuals as well as groups and are influenced by social and cultural conditions. They can produce integration or opposition. Cooperation, accommodation and assimilation are generally described as associative processes, while competition and conflict are dissociative processes.

Social processes also show continuity and change. Cooperation and established norms create continuity in social life, while competition, conflict and new conditions can lead to change. A society therefore does not remain completely stable or completely unstable. Social life develops through the continuing interaction of forces that maintain relationships and forces that transform them.

The study of social processes helps Sociology explain how people live together, adjust to differences, compete for resources, experience conflict and create new forms of social organization.

The classification of social processes into associative and dissociative processes is found in the work of many sociologists, including Ogburn and Nimkoff and Kingsley Davis. Park and Burgess identified four main processes: competition, conflict, accommodation and assimilation.

Park and Burgess suggested a sequence: competition, if it becomes personal and intense, turns into conflict; conflict is resolved through accommodation; and accommodation over a long period may lead to assimilation. This sequence is not always followed in reality but helps to understand how processes are linked.
Different sociological perspectives emphasise different processes: functionalists emphasise cooperation and integration, while conflict theorists emphasise competition, conflict and domination.

Examples from Indian society include cooperation in self-help groups, competition in examinations and elections, conflict between communities, accommodation through peace agreements, and gradual assimilation of migrants into urban culture.

sections.title: Associative Social Processes: Cooperation, Accommodation and Assimilation

blocks.text:
Associative social processes promote adjustment, integration and coordinated social relationships. The major associative processes in the syllabus are cooperation, accommodation and assimilation.

Cooperation occurs when individuals or groups work together for a common objective. Social life would be impossible without cooperation because families, institutions and communities depend upon coordinated action.

Accommodation is adjustment between individuals or groups after disagreement or conflict. It enables them to maintain workable relationships even when their differences are not completely removed. Accommodation can therefore reduce open conflict and restore a degree of stability.

Assimilation is a deeper process of integration in which individuals or groups gradually share common cultural patterns through prolonged contact. It may involve the adoption or exchange of language, values, customs or ways of life.

These processes differ in degree but all contribute to social integration. Cooperation involves working together, accommodation involves adjustment, and assimilation involves greater cultural integration.
Kropotkin, in 'Mutual Aid' (1902), argued that cooperation, not just competition, is a major factor in evolution and survival. Cooperation is the most basic and pervasive social process.

Accommodation is a temporary or permanent settlement of conflict without necessarily changing attitudes, while assimilation is a deeper and slower change in attitudes, values and identity. Accommodation can be quick and conscious, whereas assimilation is gradual and largely unconscious.

Examples: cooperation in a Mizo village community clearing a path; accommodation in agreements between rival groups or in peace accords; assimilation in the case of migrants who adopt the language and customs of their new society over generations.
In conclusion, associative processes help integrate society, maintain harmony and allow groups with different interests to live together.

sections.title: Dissociative Social Processes: Conflict, Competition and Hegemony

blocks.text:
Dissociative social processes involve opposition, rivalry or unequal relations. The syllabus identifies conflict, competition and hegemony as important forms.

Competition occurs when individuals or groups seek the same limited goals or resources. It may occur in education, employment, markets and politics. Competition can encourage effort and achievement but may also create inequality and tension.

Conflict is more direct opposition arising from incompatible interests, goals or values. It may occur between individuals, groups, classes or communities. Conflict can disturb social order, but it may also expose grievances and contribute to social change.

Hegemony refers to a form of dominance in which a powerful group maintains leadership partly by influencing ideas and gaining social consent, rather than relying only on coercion.

These processes show that social life contains not only cooperation but also rivalry and unequal power. Sociology studies both sides in order to understand the complexity of social relationships.

Differences between competition and conflict: competition is impersonal, continuous, unconscious and governed by rules, while conflict is personal, intermittent, conscious and may break rules. In competition attention is on the goal; in conflict attention is on the opponent.

Marx and Dahrendorf saw conflict as central to social change, while Coser and Simmel noted the functions of conflict in creating group boundaries and solidarity. Gramsci's concept of hegemony explains how dominance can be maintained through consent rather than open conflict.

Dissociative processes are not always harmful. Competition can encourage excellence and conflict can lead to reform. However, uncontrolled conflict can cause violence, destruction and disorganization.
Sociology therefore studies both associative and dissociative processes, since every society contains both cooperation and opposition.

sections.title: Social Disorganization: Concept, Causes, Characteristics and Remedies

blocks.text:
Social disorganization refers to a condition in which established norms, relationships and institutions become weak or ineffective in regulating social behaviour. It can appear when social change is so rapid or disruptive that existing institutions are unable to adjust effectively.

Possible causes include rapid social change, economic insecurity, conflicting norms, migration, weakening of community relationships and failures of major social institutions. The exact causes differ according to the social setting.

Its characteristics may include weakened social control, instability, conflict between norms, poor coordination among institutions and uncertainty about expected behaviour. Social disorganization may therefore affect both individuals and communities.

Remedial measures should address the conditions producing the problem. Strengthening families, schools and community institutions, improving welfare and education, reducing severe social and economic problems, promoting community participation and maintaining fair formal social control can contribute to social organization and stability.

Elliott and Merrill's 'Social Disorganization' (1934) is a classic work on the subject. Thomas and Znaniecki's study of Polish peasant migrants showed how migration weakened traditional controls and led to family breakdown and delinquency.

Criticism: some sociologists argue that the term 'disorganization' is value-laden, because what appears disorganized may simply be a different form of organization. Later writers preferred concepts such as 'deviance' and 'social problems'.
Social disorganization and social organization are relative; every society has elements of both. Rapid change does not always cause disorganization if institutions adapt quickly.

In conclusion, students should define social disorganization, explain causes (with Durkheim's anomie and Ogburn's cultural lag), describe characteristics and types (personal, family, community), and suggest practical remedies.
The Semester II multidisciplinary paper covers Family, Marriage and Kinship with emphasis on characteristics, types, functions, importance, changes, terminology, inheritance and descent.
SOC/MD/105 is the Semester II multidisciplinary paper. It is a shorter version of SOC/MJ/103 and focuses on family, marriage and kinship in a simpler form.
Students can use the notes under SOC/MJ/103 for detail, and should give special attention to inheritance, which is added under the Kinship unit of this paper.

Family is based on socially recognized relationships, has a degree of permanence, provides a common social identity and normally involves duties of care, support and socialization. Its exact form differs between societies.

MacIver and Page listed the distinctive characteristics of the family as universality, emotional basis, limited size, formative influence, nuclear position in the social structure, responsibility of members and social regulation.
The family combines biological, economic, emotional and cultural aspects. It is both an institution (a set of norms) and a group (actual members).
Although the family is universal, its form, size and authority patterns vary greatly from society to society.
Family change may involve household size, authority, residence, gender roles and relations between generations. Urbanization, education, migration and employment are important influences.

Changes in the Indian family include a shift from joint to nuclear households in many areas, greater equality between husband and wife, decline of the authority of elders, increased education and employment of women, and later marriages.

Laws such as the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, and the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, have also influenced family relations.
Despite these changes, the family continues to be important for emotional support and care, and kinship ties continue to be maintained across distance.
Marriage provides social recognition to the relationship between spouses and helps organize family formation, kinship, reproduction, inheritance and social responsibilities.
Marriage gives legitimacy to children (Malinowski's principle of legitimacy), creates alliances between families, regulates sexual behaviour and establishes rights over property and inheritance.
It gives the couple adult status and new roles as husband and wife, and later as parents.
Marriage also strengthens social integration by linking families, clans and sometimes villages.

Changes in marriage include increasing individual choice, changes in age at marriage, altered expectations of spouses and changing attitudes towards divorce and remarriage. Patterns vary across communities.

In India, important changes include the rising age at marriage, legal prohibition of child marriage and dowry, more inter-caste and love marriages in urban areas, and growing acceptance of divorce and widow remarriage.
Online matrimonial sites, migration and education have widened the choice of partners.
In Mizoram, marriage practices have combined traditional customs such as bride price with Christian church weddings, and legal reforms have addressed divorce and inheritance.

Inheritance refers to the transfer of property, rights or social positions from one generation to another according to recognized rules. Inheritance rules are often closely connected with family, kinship and descent systems.

Types of inheritance include patrilineal inheritance (property passes through males), matrilineal inheritance (property passes through females, as among the Khasi, where the youngest daughter traditionally inherits the ancestral house), primogeniture (inheritance by the eldest son) and ultimogeniture (inheritance by the youngest son).

In traditional Mizo society, the youngest son usually inherited the father's house and property and was expected to care for his parents in their old age, an example of ultimogeniture within a patrilineal system.

In India, inheritance among Hindus is governed by the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, amended in 2005 to give daughters equal rights. Christians are generally governed by the Indian Succession Act, 1925, while tribal communities may follow customary law.

For long-answer preparation in SOC/MD/105, students may use the detailed Semester II notes above on Family, Marriage, Kinship, Descent and changing patterns. The multidisciplinary syllabus asks for the same core institutions in a shorter three-unit structure, with inheritance added under Kinship.

For long answers in this multidisciplinary paper, students should prepare the following topics: definition and characteristics of family, types and functions of family, changes in family; definition, forms, importance and changes of marriage; and kinship, kinship terminology, descent and inheritance.

Including examples from Mizo and other North-East Indian societies, such as patrilineal clans, bride price and ultimogeniture, and matrilineal inheritance among the Khasi, makes answers more relevant and earns credit.
